correctness.rationale: Checked RESULT.md lines 23–43 for arbitrary T, including the empty set. The subgroup generated by the clocks is dense, cyclic discrete, or zero. In the dense case strong continuity gives all real characters in the von Neumann algebra; the multiplication spectral calculus recovers all bounded Lebesgue multipliers. In the cyclic case, functional calculus for e^{iax} gives precisely the essentially periodic multipliers of period 2π/a. In the zero case the algebra is scalar, consistent with all-shift invariance: translation-invariant L∞ functions have constant convolutions with every smooth mollifier and hence are constant almost everywhere. The resolvent symbol runs on the circle of radius and center 1/(2α), which proves both scalar upper bounds. A Bohr recurrent uniform limit of sampled trigonometric polynomials must approximate the value at β and simultaneously recur along shifts to infinity, where the symbol tends to zero. This forces error at least 1/(2α). For a nonzero alias period p the same comparison uses the countable intersection of full-measure sets for x and x+np, so no point evaluation of an L∞ class is needed. The factorial clocks give period 2πN! at each finite stage and intersection {0}; Kaplansky density gives bounded strong approximants in the dense case, not norm approximants. Inspected the finite rational checker without executing it; the subgroup, recurrence and operator-distance arguments are analytic.

value.rationale: The exact norm barrier persists even with every positive clock, despite exact measurable recovery from two irrationally related clocks. Separating stable uniform processing from measurable recovery is a natural sampling question, and the factorial example makes the finite-to-countable change precise. Combining sharp distances and the complete criterion has value beyond the particular integer divisibility example or the individual textbook tools.
